## The idea

A printed melody presents pitch, time, grouping, spelling, and expression in one
compact image. Trying to decode all of them in a single pass makes errors hard
to locate. You can copy every pitch correctly and still produce malformed bars;
you can also spend time refining a synth while the underlying transcription is
still changing.

Use a stable sequence of passes: time signature, key signature, rhythm, pitches,
ties, then articulation. Each pass enriches the same score data and leaves a
specific kind of evidence to inspect. Structural checks come first, so every bar
already has the promised duration and every written accidental has an explicit
effect before sound design enters the work.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 92
use_synth :piano

# Four bars in 4/4, already resolved from a one-sharp key signature.
bars = [
  [[:g4, 1], [:a4, 1], [:b4, 1], [:d5, 1]],
  [[:c5, 0.5], [:b4, 0.5], [:a4, 1], [:g4, 2]],
  [[:d5, 1], [:c5, 1], [:b4, 0.5], [:a4, 0.5], [:fs4, 1]],
  [[:g4, 1], [:a4, 1], [:g4, 2]]
]

bars.each_with_index do |bar, index|
  total = bar.sum { |pitch, duration| duration }
  raise "bar #{index + 1} totals #{total}" unless total == 4
end

score = []
cursor = 0
bars.each do |bar|
  bar.each do |pitch, duration|
    score << {note: pitch, start: cursor, duration: duration}
    cursor += duration
  end
end

define :play_events do |events|
  cursor = 0
  events.each do |event|
    sleep event[:start] - cursor
    play event[:note], sustain: event[:duration] * 0.82,
      release: 0.08
    sleep event[:duration]
    cursor = event[:start] + event[:duration]
  end
end

puts "#{score.length} events, #{cursor} beats"
play_events score
```

The program validates all four bar totals before producing a sound. Bar two ends
with one two-beat G event, the event shape expected after two tied values have
been merged, so only one attack occurs. F-sharp in bar three records the resolved
key-signature default. By the time `play_events` receives the flattened score,
no decision about pitch spelling or metric length remains hidden in the renderer.

## Change one thing

1. Change the last duration in bar three from `1` to `0.5`. The assertion halts
   before playback, identifying a metric defect before it can masquerade as a
   tempo or phrasing problem.
2. Split bar two's final G into two one-beat events. The total remains four, so
   the metric check passes, but playback adds a second attack. Bar arithmetic
   and tie interpretation are different validations.
3. Restore the valid score, then change synth and release. The new timbre can
   alter clarity and connection, while the decoded pitches and timing remain
   available for direct inspection.

## Why it works

The time signature provides an invariant: each 4/4 bar totals four quarter-note
beats. That allows rhythm to be entered and checked before pitch. Key resolution
then combines source spelling with signature defaults to produce playable notes.
Ties merge adjacent written durations into one event, and articulation remains
a rendering choice. Every stage has a narrower responsibility than “read the
music.”

The nested bars are source-facing data because they preserve the measure
boundaries visible on the page. The flattened score is renderer-facing and uses
absolute start times. Both views derive from the same arrays. There is no second
manual transcription to drift away from the first, and a doubtful event can
still be located in its original measure.

Listening forms another validation pass rather than a reward at the end. Loop a
suspicious bar and compare it with a lawful source recording when one is
available. A correct bar total cannot detect a wrong pitch; valid Ruby cannot
detect a wrong rhythm that happens to add to four. Assertions reduce the search
space, while page and recording comparisons test kinds of fidelity the program
cannot infer.

Provenance belongs beside the score data. Record edition, page, system, and
measure even if those fields never reach Sonic Pi. When a note sounds doubtful,
that pointer leads directly back to the evidence. It also distinguishes a
faithful encoding from an editorial change made later because another articulation
or voicing serves your arrangement.

Part 9 expands that pointer into a complete source record. Leave this lesson
with page and measure coordinates attached. Lesson 42 adds edition details,
rights information, retrieval date, and a redistribution decision before the
transcription grows beyond four bars and those facts become costly to recover.

## Take it further

Choose four bars from a public-domain score and record the exact edition. Enter
meter and rhythm first, making all bar-total assertions pass before adding pitch.
Add spelling, key-signature resolution, ties, and articulation in distinct saved
versions or commits, and preserve source measure numbers in comments. Render the
events without importing a MIDI file. Finish with a short list of every point
that still needs manual comparison with the page or an authorised recording;
uncertainty recorded now is easier to resolve than certainty invented later.
